Where should private documents live on Android?
A practical home for passport scans, certificates and the files you want to keep to yourself.
Start with the copies you already have

A document can exist in your gallery, Downloads, a messaging app and a cloud backup at the same time. Moving one copy does not necessarily remove the others. Before choosing a vault, identify where the document came from and which apps may have copied or backed it up.
Choose the protection you actually need

A hidden album changes visibility. A separate locked folder adds an access boundary. An encrypted vault protects stored contents with encryption and a secret. These protections depend on the implementation and the state of your device. None makes an unlocked, compromised phone trustworthy.
Medical records, notes and everyday paperwork

People often keep letters from a clinic, test results, prescriptions, insurance details, tenancy papers and ID scans on the same phone as everything else. A private note suits the short facts: an allergy, a medication list, a policy number. A document suits the original file. In NullKey, photos and notes open inside the vault. PDFs, videos and other files stay encrypted, and you view them by exporting a readable copy, which leaves the vault’s protection. NullKey is not a medical record system and makes no claim about healthcare rules, so keep another copy of anything you cannot replace.
Keep recovery and backup separate

A recovery key helps unlock an existing vault. A backup preserves a copy of the data. To recover after a lost phone, you need a usable backup and the passphrase or recovery key that opens that backup. Store these separately from the phone.
A sensible routine

Start with sample files. Import copies, check their contents and make an encrypted backup. Restore into a separate, empty vault before removing any old app or original. NullKey stores photos, files and notes; PDFs and videos need a readable export to view in another app, outside the vault’s protection.
hidden-folder-vs-encrypted-vault
A hidden folder and an encrypted vault do different jobs.
Visibility, access controls and encryption: what to check before trusting a private folder.
Hiding is a visibility choice

An album can disappear from the usual gallery view while its files remain available elsewhere. Do not infer encryption from a hidden icon or a folder name. Check the app’s own documentation for what is encrypted, how it unlocks and what happens to backups.
Built-in tools deserve a fair look

Files by Google offers Safe Folder, while supported Samsung devices offer Secure Folder. Their capabilities and recovery behaviour differ. Start by checking the option already available on your own phone, then identify what you still need: a separate passphrase, encrypted export or an account-free workflow.
Ask four questions

What protects the stored files? Who holds the keys? What happens if I forget the secret? How will I move to another phone? Answers are more useful than labels such as “military-grade”. A vault should explain its limits as plainly as its features.
Where NullKey fits

NullKey’s public Android app uses a passphrase, an independent recovery key and encrypted backup files. It has no account and declares no internet permission. Choose it based on those specific properties, not an assumption that every built-in alternative is insecure.
backup-offline-vault
How do you back up a vault that stays offline?
An offline app still needs a recovery plan. Here is how to build one.
Offline does not mean backed up

A vault stored only on a phone can disappear with the phone. Encryption protects confidentiality; it does not protect against loss, uninstalling an app or failing storage. Plan for losing the entire device.
Save and check a fresh export

On your unlocked phone, open Settings and choose “Create encrypted backup”. In Android’s document picker choose the destination. NullKey then rereads the saved archive and checks the index, encrypted items and thumbnails against the current vault. If the app reports that the check failed, make another backup and do not rely on that file.
Export ciphertext, not a folder of originals

An encrypted vault backup preserves protected files in an export you can store elsewhere. A decrypted export creates another readable copy. Know which operation you are using. In NullKey, the whole-vault backup contains ciphertext and requires the passphrase or recovery key from that vault.
Check the backup, then practise restoring

NullKey rereads the exported archive, authenticates its index, every encrypted item segment and every thumbnail, and matches the current vault snapshot. A restore exercise with sample data also checks that you have the right secret and understand the process. Restore requires an empty vault; never erase a working vault just to try it.
Make the routine repeatable

Keep an encrypted backup away from the phone and the unlocking secret separately. Refresh the backup after important changes. Label which passphrase or recovery key belongs to older exports: changing the current vault’s credentials does not rewrite backup files you already made.
before-deleting-originals
Before deleting the original, check the copy.
A short checklist for moving private files into a vault without losing your only copy.
Importing usually makes another copy

Adding a document to a vault is different from moving it. Confirm whether your app retains the original, deletes it, or sends it to trash. Check each source app separately; a gallery and a document provider may handle deletion differently.
Verify more than the thumbnail

For photos, check orientation and detail. For documents that NullKey cannot display, a readable export can help you check the contents, but that export is outside the vault’s protection. A thumbnail alone does not show that the whole original was preserved.
Give yourself a way back

Make an encrypted backup and keep its unlocking secret available before removing your original. A recovery key alone cannot recreate deleted data. If a source is synced, understand whether a deletion will propagate to other devices or cloud storage.
Deletion is not secure erasure

Trash, backups and other apps can retain copies. Optional original removal is off by default in NullKey. It verifies eligible local copies first. Supported photos and videos need Android’s confirmation to move to trash; other supported documents can be deleted permanently. Cloud and other-app sources are kept. Deletion is not guaranteed secure erasure.
recovery-key-vs-backup
Recovery key or backup? You need both jobs covered.
One helps you unlock. The other preserves your data. They are not interchangeable.
A key opens; a backup preserves

A recovery key is another way to unlock the vault’s encrypted data. It is not a copy of those data. A backup contains the data but still needs a valid unlocking secret. Either one on its own may be useless after the phone is gone.
Match the secret to the backup

Backups preserve the vault’s state at export time. A subsequent passphrase change or recovery-key rotation does not update earlier exports. Retain the credentials needed for backups you intend to keep, using a secure storage method separate from those backups.
Walk through a sample restore

On a phone with no NullKey vault, choose Restore on the welcome screen and select the backup in Android’s file picker. Enter the passphrase or recovery key that belongs to that export. NullKey authenticates the contents before restoring and refuses to overwrite a vault already on the phone. Test with harmless sample data first.
Practise with harmless files

Create a test vault and record its recovery key. Add sample documents, export a backup, and test your recovery workflow without removing valuable data. Check that you understand both forgotten-passphrase recovery and lost-device recovery.
Keep the language precise

“Recover my password” and “restore my files” describe different problems. NullKey provides a recovery-key unlock flow and a whole-vault backup/restore flow. There is no account reset or support-held copy of your vault.
vault-without-account
What does “no account” mean for a private vault?
Less setup, fewer server dependencies, and more responsibility for your own recovery.
Start with what the app can do

An account-free vault can create and unlock encrypted storage without an email address or a remote login. That says nothing by itself about analytics, backups or other network activity. Check those separately.
NullKey’s current boundary

The public Android app has no account, no server and no INTERNET permission. Its encrypted vault lives in the app’s local storage. Android’s document picker can still let you choose an external provider for a backup, and that provider may use the network.
You own the recovery plan

There is no “email me a reset link”. Keep a recovery key for forgotten-passphrase access and encrypted backups for device loss. Losing both unlocking secrets makes existing encrypted data inaccessible; losing the data itself cannot be fixed with a key.
Check the website separately

This product website includes Google Analytics, which stays off until you accept it in the consent banner. See Alvento’s website privacy notice for details. Its hosting infrastructure may process request and operational information. The app privacy policy is published at alvento.uk/nullkey/privacy/; the app’s lack of internet permission does not describe how a browser or website works.

How to keep private photos on Android
A practical way to organise private photos, understand Android’s locked folders and keep a recoverable copy.
Decide what “private” needs to mean

A hidden album keeps photos out of a usual gallery view, but may not encrypt the files. A locked folder adds an access check; an encrypted vault protects stored contents using encryption and a secret. Check the exact behaviour on your Android version and phone.
Check the copies you already have
Before importing, look for copies in your camera roll, messaging apps, downloads and any photo sync service you use. Moving one copy does not remove the others. Keep the originals while you test.
Import and check with sample photos first

Install NullKey from Google Play, create a vault and use Android’s picker to import a few sample photos. Unlock the vault and inspect the photos at full size. Importing keeps originals by default; do not enable removal until you understand which local copies can be affected.
Make a backup you can restore

Create a whole-vault encrypted backup and wait for NullKey’s automatic read-back check to confirm it was saved and checked. Keep the backup away from the phone and its matching passphrase or recovery key separately. Practise restoring sample photos into an empty test vault before entrusting it with anything irreplaceable.
Keep expectations realistic

A vault cannot protect a photo while it is visible on an unlocked or compromised device, remove every copy made by another app, or guarantee secure erasure. Cloud providers and Android features have their own storage and recovery rules.
restore-nullkey-backup-new-phone
How to restore a NullKey backup on a new Android phone
Move a verified NullKey backup to a new phone without removing the old app or risking the only copy.
Before changing phones

On the old phone, unlock NullKey and open Settings, then choose “Create encrypted backup”. Save the file with Android’s document picker. Wait for NullKey’s read-back check to say the backup was saved and checked. Keep the matching passphrase or recovery key separately from the backup.
Install and choose Restore

Install the current NullKey app from Google Play on the new phone. Open it to the welcome screen and choose Restore. Android’s document picker opens; select the backup file you copied to a destination available on the new device.
Unlock the backup and inspect the vault

Enter the passphrase or recovery key used for that backup. Restore authenticates the archive before installing it and requires that no vault already exists on the new phone. Unlock the restored vault and check several photos, files and notes. Restoring turns off optional biometric, screen-lock and pattern unlock settings; set those up again only after confirming the vault works.
Keep the old phone until you are sure

Do not uninstall NullKey or clear its storage on the old phone. Keep the verified backup and its matching secret until you have checked the new vault and made a fresh backup. After restoring with the passphrase, unlock the vault and save the new recovery key when prompted. It replaces the restored vault’s recovery key once you confirm it. Restoring with the recovery key keeps that key. Older backup files are unchanged; keep their matching secrets separately.
Older package IDs need extra care

This flow describes restoring a backup made by the current NullKey app. Earlier Cellar and NullKey package IDs install separately, and compatibility of their old backups with the current Play app has not been verified. Keep the old app and data; contact support with app versions to confirm a path before changing anything.
